lesson.title: Counting from the End: Negative Indices
lesson.summary: Negative indices count backward from the end of a string, with -1 referring to the last character, giving a clean way to reach trailing characters without knowing the string's length.
lesson.body:
Positive indices count forward from the start of a string, but very often the character you care about is defined by its distance from the end instead, the last letter of a word, the final digit of a phone number, the extension at the tail of a filename. Counting forward to reach these would require first knowing exactly how long the string is, which is inconvenient when the length varies or is not known in advance. Python solves this with negative indices: word[-1] refers to the last character, word[-2] refers to the second-to-last character, and so on, counting backward from the end.

Take the same string used for positive indexing, "PYTHON". Its negative indices run in the opposite direction from its positive ones: N sits at index -1, O at index -2, H at index -3, T at index -4, Y at index -5, and P at index -6. Every character in the string is reachable by two different indices, one positive and one negative, and both point to the exact same character in memory; negative indexing does not create new characters or copies, it is simply an alternate way of naming a position that already exists.

Here is negative indexing in action:

word = "PYTHON"
print(word[-1])
print(word[-3])

The first line outputs N, the last character in the string. The second outputs H, since counting backward from the end, -1 is N, -2 is O, and -3 is H. Compare this to positive indexing: word[3] also returns H, because "PYTHON" happens to be six characters long and index -3 always corresponds to index length-minus-3 for a string of that length. In general, for a string of length n, negative index -k refers to the same character as positive index n - k. Later in this unit you will meet the len() function, which reports a string's length directly, and once you have it, word[-1] turns out to be exactly equivalent to word[len(word) - 1], just without needing to look up the length or do the subtraction yourself.

Negative indexing follows the same strict boundaries as positive indexing, just mirrored. "PYTHON" has six characters, so valid negative indices run from -1 through -6; asking for word[-7] raises an IndexError for the same reason word[6] does, there simply is no character that far from either end. Index 0 and index -6 both refer to the same first character P in this six-character string, and it is worth double-checking that overlap when you are close to the edges of a string in your own code.

This backward-counting trick becomes especially valuable once you know a string's length: rather than working out and writing the last valid position by hand every time you want the last character of a string, negative indexing lets you write the far simpler and more readable word[-1], and this same convenience carries over directly into string slicing, where negative numbers can mark either the start or the stop of a range of characters.
